summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the latest measured period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more consistently tracked sectors in the federal data. The gain is modest but steady, and it spans a broad industry that includes residential brokerage, commercial property management, institutional investment, and iBuying, each of which deploys AI in meaningfully different ways.

The oldest and most consequential use is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network-based model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical sales data, with Zestimates for most homes updating multiple times per week. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics covering more than 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition technology that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor takes valuation a step further by using pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, putting real balance-sheet exposure behind the model's output. These consumer-facing and institutional tools sit at the center of the sector's AI story, and they are now subject to binding federal rules: the FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers, requiring institutions to adopt policies ensuring high confidence in AVM estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and reviews.

Beyond valuation, the sector's AI deployment branches into operations and workflow. EliseAI offers an agentic conversational AI platform that handles leasing inquiries, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests around the clock, with the platform integrating into existing property management systems. Building Engines, a JLL company, markets its Prism platform as an AI-powered tool for running commercial building operations end to end, promising smarter decisions, cost reductions, and net operating income growth from data teams already have. Prophia applies AI to commercial lease abstraction, extracting key terms and combining machine learning output with expert validation to produce structured lease data for owners and operators managing complex portfolios. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models using cameras and computer vision, enabling virtual tours, floor plan generation, and portfolio management that incorporates real-time data to cut costs and improve productivity.

On the enterprise and investment side, JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics. Compass integrates AI into residential brokerage workflows, covering agent tools, client matching, and listing recommendations. CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, maintains a network of more than 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies, representing the organized capital infrastructure behind the sector's startup layer. CREtech convenes what it describes as the world's premier real estate AI conference, drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, which signals the degree to which commercial real estate has institutionalized its AI conversation at the executive level.

The regulatory picture is the sharpest it has ever been for this sector. The interagency AVM rule is the first binding federal framework for what has been the sector's core AI application for years, and the CFPB's involvement means consumer protection and fair-lending concerns are explicitly part of the compliance requirement. Valuation bias and model accountability are now supervised matters, not voluntary commitments, which raises the compliance cost and governance burden for any institution relying on automated models in mortgage decisions. BOMA, the Building Owners and Managers Association, provides advocacy and education for commercial property operators navigating these and other regulatory trends across building operations.

For a decision-maker evaluating AI deployment in real estate, the clearest signal from these sources is that the technology is already embedded in the sector's most financially consequential process, automated valuation, and that federal regulators have responded with formal quality control requirements. Operational applications in leasing communication, lease abstraction, and building management are maturing and commercially available from multiple vendors. The investment and conference infrastructure described by CRETI and CREtech suggests active vendor competition, which tends to favor buyers. The regulatory posture, however, means that any use touching mortgage collateral valuation carries compliance obligations that require documented policies, testing, and controls, and organizations without those frameworks should treat them as a prerequisite rather than an afterthought.
